title: HTMX or Alpine.js
bottom_line: When Claude adds interactivity to a server-rendered app, it uses HTMX for anything the server owns and Alpine.js for short-lived browser-only behaviour.

sections.heading: It runs on its own, or you can call it

blocks.caption: The command takes no arguments. You rarely need it: the skill activates automatically.

cards.title: Automatic
cards.text: The skill activates on its own when Claude writes frontend code in a server-rendered context. No explicit invocation needed.

terms.definition: An app whose server builds the HTML pages and sends them to the browser.
A library where the server fetches and swaps in HTML.
A library for local browser state, such as whether a menu is open.
Information the page depends on, such as search results or whether a dropdown is open.
Single-page application: an app that runs mostly in the browser, built with a framework such as React or Vue.

blocks.title: When it activates
items: Form submission, CRUD operations, search, filtering, pagination
Any scenario where you'd otherwise reach for custom JavaScript

blocks.text: It applies even if you never mention HTMX or Alpine.js, and Claude applies it before reaching for custom JavaScript in a server-rendered context.

blocks.title: Requirements
blocks.text: None. The skill is guidance only, and needs no environment variables. It applies to projects that render HTML on the server and load HTMX and Alpine.js in the page.

sections.heading: Two questions decide which tool Claude uses

blocks.title: How Claude picks

nodes.label: Should it survive a page refresh?

blocks.caption: Server-owned or lasting state goes to HTMX. Temporary browser state goes to Alpine.js.

rows: 2. Should this survive a page refresh?

blocks.title: The idea behind each tool
items: HTMX: the server drives state and renders HTML. The browser is a dumb terminal.
Alpine.js: the browser drives ephemeral UI state. No server round-trip needed.
Use both together: HTMX fetches server-rendered fragments, and Alpine.js enhances interactivity inside those fragments.
If still unsure, Claude defaults to HTMX for data and state, and Alpine.js for presentation and interactivity.

blocks.text: When you build a server-rendered app and need to add interactivity, Claude often has to decide whether a feature should be driven by HTMX (the server fetches and swaps HTML) or Alpine.js (local browser state).
This decision framework is there so Claude consistently picks the right tool, and explains why.

sections.heading: Example: a live search box and a row menu

blocks.text: You ask Claude: "Add a search box above the orders table that filters as I type, and a dropdown menu on each row." Claude splits the work by who owns the state.

cards.title: Search box: HTMX
cards.text: The search results come from the database, so the search box uses HTMX to ask the server for the filtered table and swap it in.

cards.title: Row menu: Alpine.js
cards.text: Whether a row's dropdown is open matters only in the browser, so the menu uses Alpine.js and makes no request.

blocks.title: The search box (HTMX)
blocks.code:
<input type="search" name="q"
       hx-get="/orders" hx-trigger="input changed delay:300ms"
       hx-target="#orders-table">

sections.heading: HTMX is for anything the server should own or render

rows: Server is the source of truth

blocks.text: In short: form submissions, database queries, authenticated UI, multi-step workflows and real-time updates from the backend.

sections.heading: Alpine.js is for local, visual, short-lived behaviour

blocks.text: In short: open/close dropdowns, show/hide modals, tabs, copy-to-clipboard and transient UI polish.

sections.heading: The two work together inside one feature

nodes.label: HTMX loads the panel
nodes.note: The server owns which notifications exist.

nodes.label: Alpine.js expands one
nodes.note: The browser owns whether a notification is expanded.

blocks.text: HTMX fetches and swaps server-rendered HTML fragments. Alpine.js adds interactivity inside those fragments.

sections.heading: HTMX comes first; custom JavaScript is the exception

steps.title: HTMX is the primary model
steps.text: For standard apps (dashboards, admin tools, internal tools, forms, business apps), HTMX is the primary interaction model.

steps.title: Alpine.js complements it
steps.text: Alpine.js is a lightweight complement for UI behavior only.

steps.title: Custom JavaScript is rare
steps.text: Custom JavaScript should be the exception, not the rule.

blocks.title: What Claude also follows
items: Prefers server-rendered HTML over JSON APIs, and returns HTML fragments from the server, not JSON.
Makes failed requests visible to the user, never console-only.
Keeps Alpine.js scopes small and local, avoids global stores unless genuinely needed, and does not duplicate server business logic in Alpine.js.
Does not use Alpine.js for client-side routing or SPA patterns, and avoids SPA patterns unless you explicitly need them.
If the requirement calls for complex client-side state, Claude recommends a proper SPA framework rather than fighting against the server-rendered model.

blocks.text: The skill actively discourages recreating SPA patterns manually and avoids unnecessary client-side complexity.
